8644.t: BM3126: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
8644.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM3126 : Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I:
Background and overview: Overview of terminology, formulations and concepts,
Introduction of main tasks, error and performance metrics, data preparation/annotation: Components of learning, data representation, linear classification, formulation of ML problem,
Module II:
Learnability: Hoeffding's inequality, overfitting, performance/complexity, bias/variance trade-off,
End-to-End Machine Learning Project: Feature selection, Feature transformation, model selection and validation, regularisation
Module III:
Regression: Linear Regression, Polynomial Regression, Logistic Regression, Regularized Linear Models, Logistic Regression
Module IV:
SVM and kernels: Hyperplane, separation with hard margin, soft margin, support vector classification, kernel methods, support vector regression
Module V:
Unsupervised learning: Clustering, k-means algorithm, PCA

Course Objective

1 .

To understand basic concepts, algorithms and techniques of machine learning.
2 .

To develop skills for analysing data and using it for training and deploying machine learning systems.
3 .

To gain understanding of software tools used for implementation of machine learning to solve challenges in healthcare sector.

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course, the student will be able to:
1. Learn foundational understanding of machine learning concepts.
2. Understand the different statistical and probabilistic concepts which enable machines to learn.
3. Develop data pre-processing pipelines for biological and healthcare data.
4. Develop machine learning models for classification and regression tasks required in healthcare applications.
5. Optimise machine learning models for better performance and easier translation for use in healthcare applications.

Essential Reading

1 .

Hastie, Tibshirani, Freidman, The Element of Statistical Learning, Springer , First Edition

2 .

Shai Shavlev and Shai Ben-David, Understanding Machine Learning, Cambridge University Press , Second Edition

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Aurelien Geron, Hands-On Machine Learning with Sci-kit Learn, Keras and Tensorflow, O'Reilly , First

2 .

Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio, Aaron Courville, Deep Learning, The MIT Press, Cambridge Mass. , Second

8132.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ME4254 : Semiconductor Manufacturing { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I [7 h]: Introduction: Historical Evolution, Present trend, importance, classification, IC manufacturing steps, Microchip, Fundamentals of micro and nano fabrication technologies.
Semiconductor Basics and Device: Semiconductor Materials, Transport and recombination theory, pn and Schottky barrier diodes, bipolar and junction field-effect transistors, and MOS capacitors, ICs and transistors.
Semiconductor Manufacturing Environment: Contamination, its control, Clean rooms, design, Silicon Wafers, preparation, safety requirements, cleaning process, wet chemical etching techniques.
Module II [7 h]: Silicon growth: Silicon crystal structure, Defects, single crystal growth, EGS from MGs, theory, methods, preparation, required properties
Epitaxial growth: Principle, model, methods of deposition, doping and anti-doping, Substrate Engineering, MBE, Defects, Application
Oxidation: Kinetics of Silicon dioxide growth both for thick, thin and ultra-thin films, Oxidation technologies, Thermal Processes, RTP, Characterization of oxide films, Defects.
Thin Film Deposition: Synthesis and properties of various types of inorganic membranes and thin films, sol-gel process, synthesis of porous materials and thin films, Chemical and physical Vapor Deposition and Dielectric Thin Films, Metal Film Deposition: Evaporation and sputtering techniques, Failure mechanisms in metal interconnects, Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD), Deposition of Dielectrics and Semiconductor Layers.
Module III [7 h]: Diffusion: Laws, Diffusivities, systems, Impurity Incorporation, modeling.
Lithography: Photolithography, steps, optical lithography, E-beam lithography and advanced newer lithography techniques and back-end processing, Mask generation, Vapor Prime to Soft Bake, Alignment and Exposure, Photoresist Development.
Etching: classification, type, parameters, Ion beam milling, Doping, Chemical Mechanical Polishing
Module IV [7 h]: Ion Implantation: Plasma Basics, Theory, Implanters, annealing, channeling, applications.
Metalization: Single level, Multi-level metallization schemes, wiring the Chip, methods, CMP, CMOS metallization steps, problems
Module V [8 h]: Process Integration: Silicon processing, methods, Passive components, Bipolar Technology, MOSFET Technology, MESFET Technology, fabrication of p-n junction, BJT, CMOS, BiCMOS,
Introduction to MEMs: Types, characteristics, microprocessing, methods, packaging.
Assembling and Packaging: materials, types, die attachment techniques, packaging fabrication techniques, sealing, encapsulation, assembly process, techniques, reliability problems in packaging.

Course Objective

1 .

To Introduce semiconductor thin film technology for fabrication of electronic and photonic devices and integrated circuits.
2 .

To make the students familiar with the Silicon wafer preparation those are used in semiconductor industries.
3 .

To explain the different micro and nano fabrication methods used in semiconductor manufacturing.
4 .

Different advanced technologies to be explained on testing and measurements of thin film.

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1. Get the theoretical basis for processing of semiconductor devices and integrated circuits.
CO2. Able to do photolithography and simple processing of semiconductors in clean room, and to do characterization with selected techniques.
CO3. Able to present and discuss the theoretical basis for processing and characterization.
CO4. Able to process integrate the all complex activities of semiconductor manufacturing.
CO5. Able to know the advanced technologies on testing and measurements of thin film.

Essential Reading

Parasuraman Swaminathan, Semiconductor Materials, Devices and Fabrication, Wiley India , 2023

2 .

G. S. May and S. M. Sze, Fundamentals of Semiconductor Fabrication, Wiley India , 2022

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Stephen A. Campbell, The Science and Engineering of Microelectronic Fabrication, Oxford University Press , 2021

2 .

S. Franssila, Introduction to Microfabrication, Wiley-Blackwell , 2020

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE3204 : Advanced Structural Analysis { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Syllabus
Prerequisites: Undergraduate level courses on structural analysis and Mathematics of Matrix analysis
Module I: Review of concepts in structural analysis (8 hours)
Different structural elements, joints and support conditions, static indeterminacy & kinematic indeterminacy, stability, equilibrium, compatibility, force-displacement relationship, analysis of beams and frames by slope deflection method, introduction to matrix & flexibility method.
Module II: Matrix analysis of bar & spring assemblage (6 hours)
Element stiffness matrix of bar & spring assemblage, generation of global stiffness matrix, boundary condition by elimination or penalty approach, examples of bar & spring assemblage problems using direct stiffness approach, temperature stresses in bar element, stresses in bar element due to lack of fit.
Module III: Direct stiffness approach of pin jointed truss (8 hours)
Development of element stiffness matrix by direct stiffness approach, generating truss stiffness matrix by transformation matrix approach, example problems of 2D & 3D truss by stiffness approach, temperature stresses for truss.
Module IV: Stiffness approach for beam & rigid jointed frame (8 hours)
Beam element stiffness, an assemblage of element stiffness matrix to global stiffness, applying boundary conditions, examples of continuous beam problem with nodal & inter-nodal loads, direct stiffness approach for rigid jointed frames with example problems.
Module V: Force method or Flexibility matrix method (6 hours)
Developing flexibility matrix for different statically indeterminate beams with different support conditions, analysis of truss structure using flexibility approach.

Course Objective

1 .

This course will enable students to:
1. To develop a skills to idealize, formulate, and analyze determinate and indeterminate structures (beams, trusses, and frames) using classical and matrix structural analysis methods.
2 .

2. To present modern methods to determine the force distribution and
deformed shapes of structures.
3 .

3. To develop skills in interpreting and predicting solutions from structural analysis.
4 .

4. To introduce computer-based applications for the numerical methods as
presented.

Course Outcome

1 .

After the completion of this course, students will be able to:
CO1: Students will understand the basic concept of slope-deflection, stiffness & flexibility method.
CO2: Students will be able to analyse the bar & spring assemblage problems using the stiffness method.
CO3: Students will be able to solve 2D & 3D truss problems using the direct stiffness approach.
CO4: Students will be able to understand the stiffness approach for beam & rigid jointed frame structure.
CO5: Students will be able to learn applications of the flexibility method for statically indeterminate beam and truss structures.

(1) Menon, Devdas, Advanced Structural Analysis, Narosa Publication, (2) MATRIX ANALYSIS of FRAMED STRUCTURES, 3-rd Edition, by Weaver and Gere Publishe, Chapman & Hall, New York, New York, 1990, (3) Junarkar, S. B. and Shah, H. J. (1999). Mechanics of Structures – Vol. II, Charotar Publishing House, Anand

Classical Structural Analysis – A Modern Approach, McGraw-Hill Book Company, NY, ISBN 0-07-100120-4, (6) Hibbeler, R. C. (2002). Structural Analysis, Pearson Education (Singapore) Pte. Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE3202 : Design of Steel Structure { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Introduction and design approach: Properties of structural steel, Indian standard specifications and sections, analysis procedures and design philosophy, introduction to limit state design. [3 hours]
Module 2 :

Design of connections: Bolted, and welded connections, design of simple and eccentric connections. [7 hours]
Module 3 :

Design of tension members: Types of tension members, design of tension members, lug angles. [5 hours]
Module 4 :

Design of compression members: Types of compression members, design of axially loaded compression members, built-up columns, lacing, batten. [5 hours]
Module 5 :

Design of column bases: Design of solid slab base, design of gusseted base. [4 hours]
Module 6 :

Design of beams: Behaviour of steel beams, section classification, web buckling and crippling, deflection, design procedure of rolled beams, design of purlins. [6 hours]
Module 7 :

Design of plate girder: Elements of plate girder, proportioning of web and flanges, flexural strength, shear strength of web, design of stiffeners. [4 hours]

Course Objective

1 .

Students will learn the basic concept of designing steel structural elements.
2 .

Students will learn to design bolted, and welded connections.
3 .

Students will learn to design tension and compression members in steel structures.
4 .

Students will learn to design steel beams and plate girders.

Course Outcome

1 .

Students will be able to design simple bolted and welded joints in steel structure.
2 .

Students will be able to design eccentric bolted and welded joints in steel structure.
3 .

Students will be able to design steel tension members.
4 .

Students will be able to design steel compression members and column bases.
5 .

Students will be able to design steel beams and plate girders.

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CH6432 : Advanced Thermodynamics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Postulational thermodynamics: Review of basic postulates, Maxwell's relations, Legendre transformation, real fluids equilibrium, phase rule, single component phase diagrams, postulational approach to multi-component multiphase equilibrium, Gibbs-Duhem relation and energy minimum principle, alternative fundamental relations and thermodynamic potentials, stability and phase transition.
Statistical thermodynamics: Introduction to classical statistical mechanics, quantum mechanics, Canonical ensemble, microcanonical ensemble, grand canonical ensemble, Boltzmann, Fermi-dirac and Bose Einstein statistics, fluctuations, monoatomic and diatomic gases, phase space, liouville equation, Crystals, intermolecular forces and potential energy functions, imperfect monoatomic gases.
Molecular thermodynamics of fluid phase equilibria: Molecular theory of corresponding states, introduction to molecular simulations, mixtures, partial molar properties, Gibbs Duhems equations, fugacity and activity coefficients, Ideal and non-ideal solutions, Molecular theories of activity coefficients, lattice models, VLE/SLE/LLE/VLLE, chemical equilibrium and combined phase and reaction equilibria, theories of solution and high pressure equilibria.

Course Objective

1 .

To make the students aware the essence of Postulational thermodynamics replacing the laws of thermodynamics with postulates so that the formalism of thermodynamics is quite general in nature and independent of heat engines and their performance thus enabling its acceptance to all branches of engineering and in almost all physical and chemical sciences.
2 .

To provide deeper understanding of classical thermodynamics through Statistical thermodynamics.
3 .

Help to grow proficiency in Multiphase and multicomponent phase equilibria modeling very often enhanced by chemical reaction equilibria
4 .

To make the students learn Energy integrated system design and exergy analysis

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Enable the students to formalize the thermodynamic problems in terms of postulates.
2. This course enables the students to have deeper understanding, hence expertise in solving problem related to Multiphase and multicomponent phase equilibrium.
3. Exergy analysis and integrated system design

Shell, M Scott,, Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics: An Integrated Approach, Cambridge University Press , 2015

8900.t: FP3401: Food Analysis and Quality Control
8900.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : FP3401 : Food Analysis and Quality Control { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Unit 1: Introduction to Food Analysis
Importance and scope of food analysis, Regulatory standards and guidelines (e.g., FDA, FSSAI), Sampling methods and preparation, Errors and quality control in food analysis
Unit 2: Chemical Analysis of Food Components
Proximate analysis (moisture, ash, protein, fat, fiber, carbohydrates), Vitamin and mineral analysis, Determination of food additives and preservatives, Analysis of flavor compounds
Unit 3: Physical and Sensory Analysis
Texture analysis and rheology, Colorimetry and spectrophotometry, Sensory evaluation techniques, Instrumental methods for sensory analysis
Unit 4: Chromatographic and Spectroscopic Techniques
Principles of chromatography (HPLC, GC, TLC), Spectroscopic methods (UV-Vis, IR, NMR, Mass Spectrometry), Applications of chromatographic and spectroscopic techniques in food analysis,
Data interpretation and troubleshooting
Unit 5: Microbiological and Contaminant Analysis
Methods for detecting microbial contamination in food, Analysis of foodborne pathogens, Detection of chemical contaminants (pesticides, heavy metals, mycotoxins), Risk assessment and management of food contaminants

Course Objective

1 .

To provide comprehensive knowledge about the principles and methods of food analysis.
2 .

To understand the various techniques used for analyzing the chemical composition, physical properties, and contaminants in food.
3 .

To develop skills for selecting appropriate analytical methods and instruments for specific food components.
4 .

To interpret and evaluate analytical data in the context of food quality and safety standards.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Students will be able to describe the principles and applications of various analytical techniques used in food analysis.
2. Students will gain proficiency in the use of laboratory instruments and methods for analyzing food components.
3. Students will be able to critically analyze and interpret data obtained from food analysis experiments.
4. Students will demonstrate the ability to apply food analysis techniques to ensure food quality and safety.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : MA4102 : Measure Theory { 3-1-0 / 4}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I (10 hours)
Lebesgue outer measure, Measurable sets and Lebesgue measure, Non-measurable sets, Semi-algebras, algebras, monotone class, sigma-algebras, Borel sets.
Module II (12 hours)
Measurable functions, Simple functions, Littlewood’s three principles, Lebesgue integral, Fatou’s lemma, Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem, Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem,
Module III (6 hours)
Lp spaces, Minkowski's and Holder's inequalities, Completeness of Lp spaces,
Module IV (12 hours)
Convergence in measure, Differentiation of monotone functions, Functions of bounded variation, Absolute continuity, Abstract measure spaces, Completion of measure, Product measure, Fubini’s theorem.

Course Objective

1 .

To introduce the concept of Lebesgue integral via Lebesgue measure on real line, and extend this idea to higher dimensional Euclidean spaces and abstract spaces.

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1. Students will be able to understand the limitations of Riemann integration and the need of extension of the concept of length/volume to measure.
CO2. They will get acquainted with the Lebesgue integral and related results.
CO3. They will be able to do manipulations/interchanges related to sums and integral.
CO4. They will learn the properties of Lp spaces.
CO5. They will learn about different types of convergence and relation between them along with extensions of fundamental results of calculus of one variable.

Essential Reading

1 .

H. L. Royden, Real Analysis, Macmillan Publishing Company

2 .

G. De Barra, Measure Theory and Integration, Ellis Horwood Publishing Corporation

Supplementary Reading

1 .

E. D. Benedetto, Real Analysis: Foundations and Applications, Springer

2 .

I. K. Rana, An Introduction to Measure and Integration, Narosa Publishing House
